study.title: Proverbs 21 - righteousness, dominion of God, and practical wisdom
study.overview: Proverbs 21 gathers short sayings that confront human self-sufficiency and show that God rules the king's heart, weighs human hearts and determines the final outcome of actions. The chapter opposes justice to empty sacrifice, humility to pride, generosity to avarice, laziness and confidence in human resources to dependence on the Lord. The general message is practical and moral: true wisdom appears less in religious words and more in integrity, mercy, dominion of the language and fear of God.

outline.title: God rules kings, weigh hearts, and judges ways
outline.explanation: The first proverbs claim that the king's heart is in the hands of the LORD and that no one evaluates himself with total impartiality; God is the one who weighs the intentions. Here it is also noteworthy that justice is worth more than sacrifice, and that pride, uncontrolled haste and lies produce ruin. The contrast between the path of the wicked and the work of the pure prepares the reader to understand that the exterior appearance does not replace the inner uprightness.

outline.title: Domestic conflict, discipline and compassion for the poor
outline.explanation: This section brings together sayings about the quarrelsome woman, the evil desire of the wicked, the usefulness of correction and the need for mercy. The righteous learns by observing the fall of the wicked, but hardening against the poor brings a principle of retribution: whoever closes his ears to the cry of others should not expect to be heard. The contrast between the joy of the just and fear of the wicked shows that justice is not mere duty, but pleasure for the whole.

outline.title: Excessive pleasure, domestic wisdom and speech care
outline.explanation: The proverbs here warn that love of pleasure and consumption leads to need, while wisdom manages resources well. It also emerges the replacement of the perverse by the just as a matter of judgment, and again the text compares life in peace with coexistence with a trustees. The chapter then directs to language: to keep mouth and tongue preserves the soul, while the arrogant and mockery reveals its character through the offensive posture.

outline.title: Laziness, falsehood, perseverance, and the victory that comes from the LORD
outline.explanation: The final passage denounces the desire that paralyzes the lazy, the lie of the false witness and the hardness of the wicked. It is then said that there is no wisdom, understanding, or counsel against the LORD, and at last that the horse can be prepared for battle, but victory belongs to God. The closure summarizes the chapter: human planning is real, but subordinate to the divine government.

study.context: The notes presented place the book in the environment of known kings and agricultural and domestic practices in the ancient world. The commentary on the king in verse 1 uses the image of irrigation channels to explain God's sovereignty over human decisions; verse 31 uses the horse as a symbol of military force. The chapter, however, does not depend on broad historical details for his main message: he insists that God directs, weighs and decides.
study.theology: The chapter teaches God's active sovereignty over rulers, hearts, and results. This does not nullify human responsibility, for the text insists on justice, mercy, diligent work, honesty and dominion of speech. Outer religion does not replace moral obedience; sacrifice without righteousness is rejected. There is also a strong theology of moral retribution: the path of the wicked tends to ruin, while the righteous finds life, honor and divine help. Finally, the ultimate victory does not depend on human force or strategic intelligence, but on the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The heart of the king is in the hand of God, who can direct him despite his apparent power.
Practicing justice and mercy is more pleasing to God than the most eye-catching religious sacrifice, because moral duty has priority over rite.
Even with the horse prepared for battle, security and victory belong to the LORD, not military force.

questions: In which areas can I be relying on religious appearance or human planning, rather than practicing justice in a concrete way?
Does my way of speaking preserve the soul and promote peace, or expose pride and conflict?
Where have I resisted the idea that God weighs my intentions, and not just my external actions?
study.practice: This week, choose three practices from Proverbs 21: to take concrete action of justice for someone vulnerable, watch impulsive words before answering, and handing over to God an area in which you try to control everything by self-force. If there is a family or domestic conflict, give priority to peace and meekness before insisting on winning the discussion. When planning study, work or decisions, do his part diligently, but pray recognizing that the final result depends on the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The chapter uses sapiential and proverbial language, so several sentences are general and do not describe mechanical promises. The given notes illuminate only a few verses; where there is no commentary, the reading was built only from the biblical text of the chapter. It is also not possible to affirm with certainty, from the notes, wide historical details about composition, dates or specific scenario of the proverb.
